Issued at 233 PM CDT Sun Sep 13 2026

Rest of Today - Tonight:

High pressure is solidly in place over the Upper Midwest, with
partly cloudy skies this afternoon due to diurnal cumulus
clouds. High temperatures top out near 60F to the upper 60s,
warmest in Pine County to northwest WI. A few diurnal
sprinkles/very light showers are possible near the international
border/tip of the Arrowhead through early evening, but little to
no accumulations are expected. Daytime west to northwest winds
with gusts to 20 mph become light this evening.

Calm to light winds and clear skies for most of the Northland
tonight will allow for good radiational cooling. This will push
low temperatures tonight into early Monday morning down into the
low to mid 30s, coolest in inland northeast MN and northwest 
Wisconsin. The typical cold spots in inland northwest WI and
northeast MN could even touch freezing or slightly below
freezing for a couple hours towards sunrise early Monday
morning. Widespread freezing temperatures are not anticipated,
so will maintain Frost Advisories with this forecast update. Warmer
temperatures in the upper 30s to low/mid 40s are expected near 
Lake Superior, and in the Brainerd Lakes due to increasing high 
cloud cover ahead of an approaching low pressure system on 
Monday.

Monday - Tuesday:

The high pressure will be departing to our east early Monday as
a strengthening and increasingly vertically-stacked low pressure
system over Montana early Monday slides northeast into southern
Manitoba Monday evening and far northwest Ontario Monday night
into early Tuesday. An attendant surface occluded front with
this system will also be moving west to east across the
Northland late Monday evening and night. Expect strong moisture
advection ahead of this system/front, leading to strong
isentropic ascent and widespread rain showers with embedded
thunderstorms spreading from southwest to northeast across the
Northland from late Monday morning through afternoon. Showers
and embedded thunderstorms continue into Monday evening and
night, ending from west to east as the occluded front sweeps
through. While severe weather is not expected, some elevated
instability (MUCAPE around 200-500 J/kg), being highest in Pine
County to northwest WI, combined with marginal lapse rates aloft
(6 degC/km or less) and strong bulk shear vectors in the late
afternoon and evening could lead to some small hail (pea size 
to one-half inch). Since a surface inversion should remain in
place, strong thunderstorm winds are not expected. However,
gusty southeast synoptic winds increasing throughout the day
will reach upwards of 35 mph in the afternoon and evening hours
and accompany the precipitation. 

Speaking of precipitation, the current deterministic rainfall
forecast calls for amounts of 0.3-1.25" on Monday into Monday
night, being lowest (0.3-0.5") north of the Iron Range, and
higher along/south of the Iron Range. While most locations south
of the Iron Range should top out at around or less than 1", 
both NBM >1" probabilities (60-80%) and HREF 24-hour LPMM 
highlight areas of the Brainerd Lakes and east-central Minnesota
into the Twin Ports/parts of the North Shore that could see 
upwards of 1.5". These higher amounts would be tied to higher 
rainfall rates associated with any embedded thunderstorms that 
could lead to some ponding of water on urban surfaces. Given 
that these areas are not co- located with where recent heavy 
rains fell Friday night, flooding concerns remain low. 

Expect strong west to northwest winds with gusts up to 30 to
locally 40 mph on Tuesday behind the occluded front, gradually 
decreasing late in the day. Slightly below seasonal high
temperatures in the low 60s to around 70F are forecast for
Tuesday. Light winds and mainly clear skies Tuesday night as
high pressure settles overhead will bring cooler low
temperatures back into the area in the upper 30s to mid 40s.
Can't rule out some mid-30s in the typical cold spots, but the
potential for more widespread frost appears low (less than 30%
chance) at this time.

Mid-Week into Next Weekend:

A primarily zonal flow pattern aloft sets up for Wednesday
through the end of the work week. High pressure should keep most
of Wednesday dry, though rain shower chances (10-40%) return
Wednesday night. Additional precipitation chances are forecast
for Friday into early Saturday as lee cyclogenesis develops a 
surface low and ejects it northeast. There is some uncertainty 
as to how far north the low pressure and its associated moisture
makes it into the Upper Midwest, so have maintained the broader
NBM precipitation chances of 30-55% across the region for now. 
Should this system take a more northern track, the Northland 
could be poised to get another round of much needed rainfall.
